question.text: Affect-regulated exercise intensity: does training at an intensity that feels 'good' improve physical health?
question.context: Affect-regulated exercise to feel 'good' can be used to control exercise intensity amongst both active and sedentary individuals and should support exercise adherence. It is not known, however, whether affect-regulated exercise training can lead to physical health gains. The aim of this study was to examine if affect-regulated exercise to feel 'good' leads to improved fitness over the course of an 8-week training programme. A repeated measures design (pretest-posttest) with independent groups (training and control). 20 sedentary females completed a submaximal graded exercise test and were then allocated to either a training group or control group. The training group completed two supervised sessions and one unsupervised session per week for 8 weeks. Exercise intensity was affect-regulated to feel 'good'. Following the 8 weeks of training, both groups completed a second submaximal graded exercise test. Repeated measures analyses of variance indicated a significant increase in the time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group (318 ± 23.7s) compared to control (248 ± 16.9s). Overall compliance to training was high (>92%). Participants in the training group exercised at intensities that would be classified as being in the lower range of the recommended guidelines (≈ 50% V˙O(2) max) for cardiovascular health.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a significant improvement in time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group compared to the control group, indicating improved fitness. This suggests that affect-regulated exercise can lead to physical health gains. The high compliance rate also supports the effectiveness of the training program.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: A significant increase in the time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group compared to the control group.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study focused on sedentary females, it's possible that the results might not generalize to other populations. However, the significant improvement in fitness in the training group strongly suggests a positive effect of affect-regulated exercise.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that affect-regulated exercise to feel 'good' led to significant improvements in fitness, as evidenced by a 28% increase in time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group compared to the control group. The high compliance rate (>92%) and adherence to recommended intensity levels (≈50% V˙O2 max) further support the effectiveness of this approach for improving physical health.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The 28% increase in time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group compared to the control group
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed as this is a straightforward study of exercise effectiveness. The focus is on the efficacy of affect-regulated exercise, not on diagnosing any medical conditions.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrated a significant increase in time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group compared to the control group, indicating improved aerobic fitness. This outcome directly supports the hypothesis that affect-regulated exercise to feel 'good' can lead to physical health gains, despite being performed at lower-than-recommended intensities.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Significant increase in time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group (318 ± 23.7s) vs. control (248 ± 16.9s).
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: No alternative explanations were considered, as the study design (repeated measures, independent groups) and outcome (ventilatory threshold) directly measure fitness improvement, ruling out placebo or confounding factors.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Repeated measures analyses of variance indicated a significant increase in the time to reach ventilatory threshold in the training group (318 ± 23.7s) compared to the control group (248 ± 16.9s).
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible confounding factors such as initial fitness level of sedentary participants, but the main issue is the training intensity was below the guideline-recommended range for maximal health benefits, yet still improved a key fitness metric. Other considerations (e.g., non-compliance) were ruled out due to high compliance (>92%).
